Maren came down to the flats before the light did. The tide had gone out in the night and left the mud ribbed like the roof of a mouth, silver where it held water, black where it didn't. She stood on the levee with the bucket against her hip and waited for the channel markers to show.

Cold worked through her boots. She let it.

Her mother used to say the flats gave back whatever you brought down to them. Bring patience, get clams; bring hurry, get a boot full of water and a bad afternoon. Maren had brought neither. She had brought the kind of tiredness that sleep didn't fix, and the flats took it and spread it out thin across a half mile of mud, and that was better than keeping it in her pockets.

A heron picked its way along the channel edge, lifting each leg like it was thinking about something else. She watched it hunt. Three steps, stillness, the strike. It came up empty and did not seem troubled. It went back to walking.

She dug where the sand showed its little keyholes, and the bucket filled slower than it used to when her hands were younger. That was fine. The sky went from slate to pearl to a color that had no name that she knew of, only a feeling, the one that came with the first winter she'd spent out here alone.

By the time the light was full she had enough for chowder and some over. She straightened, and her back told her about it, and she told her back it could file a complaint with the management. The tide had turned somewhere out past the markers. You couldn't see it turn. You only knew that what had been leaving was now coming back — patient as anything, the way the big slow things of the world are patient.

She climbed the levee and looked back once. The heron had its fish.

"Good," she said, to it, or to the flats, or to the day. "One of us ought to."
